entry: Natural hazard involving the downslope movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity. Landslides include rockfalls, mudflows, debris flows and shallow or deep-seated slope failures. They occur on mountain slopes, on coastal cliffs and even underwater, where they are called submarine landslides. Gravity is the main driving force, but a slope becomes unstable through factors such as saturation by rainwater or meltwater, erosion by rivers or sea waves, [[Earthquake|earthquake]] shaking, volcanic eruptions and repeated freezing and thawing. Human activity often increases the risk, through [[Deforestation|deforestation]], [[Mining|mining]], road cutting and [[Urbanization|urban sprawl]]. Mitigation includes hazard mapping, slope stabilization and early warning systems.

American poet, novelist, playwright and social activist. An early innovator of jazz poetry, Hughes is best known as a leader of the Harlem Renaissance. Born in Joplin, Missouri, he was raised mainly by his maternal grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas. He moved to [[New York City|New York City]] as a young man and studied at [[Columbia University|Columbia University]], though he dropped out; he later graduated from Lincoln University. His first poetry collection, *The Weary Blues*, appeared in 1926. He also wrote plays, short stories, novels and nonfiction. From 1942 to 1962 he wrote a weekly opinion column for *The Chicago Defender*, a leading black newspaper. He wrote extensively about [[African Americans|African American]] life, and from the 1930s he addressed labor and racial justice in his work.

Process by which humans acquire the capacity to perceive, understand and produce language. The term usually refers to first-language acquisition in infants, whether the language is spoken or signed. A child must acquire phonology, morphology, [[Syntax|syntax]], semantics and an extensive vocabulary, and [[Recursion|recursion]] allows speakers to produce an effectively infinite number of sentences. Speech perception precedes speech production, and learning builds step by step from individual phonemes. Theories have long disagreed about innate ability. [[Plato|Plato]] suggested that word-meaning mapping may be innate, while empiricists such as [[Thomas Hobbes|Thomas Hobbes]] and [[John Locke|John Locke]] held that knowledge arises from sense experience. Behaviorism, articulated by [[B. F. Skinner|B. F. Skinner]], attributed learning to reinforcement, while nativist theories associated with [[Noam Chomsky|Noam Chomsky]] posit an innate Universal Grammar. Second-language acquisition is often more effortful after early childhood.

Process in which a language loses all its native speakers. A language dies when its last native speaker dies, and it becomes extinct when no one, including second-language speakers, knows it. The forced death of a language is called linguicide. In the modern period, from about 1500, language death has typically resulted from cultural assimilation and language shift to a dominant [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]], largely those of European countries. The most common form, gradual death, occurs as speakers become bilingual and each generation's proficiency declines. A language may also survive only in religious, literary or ceremonial use, as with [[Latin|Latin]] and [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. In the 2000s roughly 7,000 languages were spoken, most of them minor languages in danger of extinction; one 2004 estimate expected some 90% to be extinct by 2050.

Group of languages related through descent from a common ancestor, called a proto-language. Daughter languages usually diverge through geographical separation, as regional dialects change in different ways. The [[Romance languages|Romance languages]], including Spanish, French, Italian and Romanian, all descend from [[Latin|Vulgar Latin]] and form part of the larger Indo-European family, the largest by number of living speakers. Relatedness is identified through shared features such as regular sound changes, which the [[Historical linguistics|comparative method]] uses to reconstruct proto-languages. Language contact can produce misleading similarities: the Mongolic, Tungusic and [[Turkic languages|Turkic]] languages were once thought to be related, but most scholars attribute the resemblances to contact. Estimates vary; Ethnologue lists 142 families, while Lyle Campbell identifies 406 independent families, including isolates. The [[Austronesian languages|Austronesian]] family contains over 1,000 languages.

Galaxy supercluster and basin of attraction, home to the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]] and about 100,000 other nearby [[Galaxy|galaxies]]. Its name is Hawaiian for 'immense heaven'. Defined in 2014 by a team of astronomers including R. Brent Tully, it is centered on the [[Great Attractor|Great Attractor]], toward which the flows of galaxies converge. It has a mass of about 10¹⁷ [[Solar mass|solar masses]]. Follow-up studies suggest it is not gravitationally bound and will eventually disperse.

Any of 15 metallic [[Chemical element|chemical elements]] with atomic numbers 57 to 71, from [[Lanthanum|lanthanum]] through lutetium. The first 14, up to [[Ytterbium|ytterbium]], fill the 4f electron shell. Lutetium is often included although it is a d-block element, and IUPAC recommends the name lanthanoid. Lanthanides usually form trivalent ions, and their chemistry depends largely on ionic radius, which decreases steadily across the series. Several can also form +2 and +4 oxidation states, such as [[Cerium|cerium]] and [[Europium|europium]]. The term [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth element]] often includes scandium, yttrium and lutetium along with the 4f elements. In periodic tables the lanthanides are customarily shown as two rows below the main body of the table.

Soft, silvery-white metal, the [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with atomic number 57 and symbol La. It is the first element of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series and is traditionally counted among the rare-earth elements. Lanthanum usually occurs with [[Cerium|cerium]] and other rare earths in minerals such as monazite and bastnäsite. Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander found it in 1839 as an impurity in cerium nitrate, and the name comes from the Greek lanthanein, 'to lie hidden'. Pure metal was not isolated until 1923. It is the 28th most abundant element in Earth's crust. Its compounds are used as catalysts, as additives in [[Glass|glass]], in carbon arc lamps for studio lights and projectors, and in ignition elements for lighters. Lanthanum carbonate treats high blood phosphate levels in kidney failure.

City, capital of Gansu province in northwestern China (pop., 2024: nearly 4.44 million). It lies on the banks of the [[Yellow River|Yellow River]] and is a key regional transport hub, historically a major link on the Northern Silk Road. Lanzhou is the geographical center of China's land territory and a center of heavy and petrochemical industry. In 81 BC, under the [[Han dynasty|Han dynasty]], it was taken from the Huns. The city acquired its current name in 1656, under the [[Qing dynasty|Qing dynasty]], and became capital of Gansu when the province was made separate in 1666. It hosts several universities, including Lanzhou University. A 2014 [[Benzene|benzene]] contamination of its water supply exposed weaknesses in urban infrastructure.

Chinese novelist and dramatist of Manchu descent, known for satirical portrayals of Beijing life. Born Shu Qingchun in Beijing to a poor Manchu family, he took the pen name Lao She. He taught in Beijing and [[Tianjin|Tianjin]] before spending 1924 to 1929 in London as a lecturer, where he absorbed [[English literature|English literature]], especially Dickens. He used the Beijing dialect in his novels and plays, and his best-known works are the novel *Rickshaw Boy* and the play *Teahouse*. In 1938 he led the All-China Resistance Association of Writers and Artists, which aimed to unite cultural workers against Japan. He spent 1946 to 1949 in the United States. During the [[Cultural Revolution|Cultural Revolution]] he was persecuted and died by drowning in Taiping Lake; accounts differ on whether it was suicide or murder.

Landlocked country in Southeast Asia, officially the Lao People's Democratic Republic (pop., 2025 census: 6,744,701). Its capital and largest city is [[Vientiane|Vientiane]]. Laos borders Myanmar, China, Vietnam, Cambodia and Thailand, and the [[Mekong|Mekong]] River forms much of its western boundary. The kingdom of [[Lan Xang|Lan Xang]] flourished from the 14th to 18th centuries as a hub for overland trade. In 1893 its kingdoms were unified under French rule as part of [[French Indochina|French Indochina]], and it regained full independence in 1953. A civil war from 1959 to 1975 ended with the establishment of the Lao People's Democratic Republic. Since then the Lao People's Revolutionary Party has governed as the sole party. Agriculture employs over 60% of the workforce, and Laos has three [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Sites]], including Luang Prabang.

Deep-blue [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rock]] valued as a gemstone since antiquity for its intense color. It is composed mainly of lazurite, with calcite and pyrite. Mined in what is now [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan]] from the 7th millennium BC, it was used in the funeral mask of Tutankhamun. From the end of the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]], Europeans ground it into the pigment [[Ultramarine|ultramarine]], used by [[Renaissance|Renaissance]] and [[Baroque|Baroque]] painters including [[Titian|Titian]] and [[Masaccio|Masaccio]], often for the robes of the Virgin Mary.

Neolithic [[Austronesian peoples|Austronesian]] culture of the Pacific, known for its dentate-stamped pottery. Lapita people settled Island Melanesia by sea from about 1600 to 500 BCE, and they are believed to have originated in the northern Philippines, directly or via the [[Mariana Islands|Mariana Islands]]. Their pottery, decorated with a toothed stamp, closely resembles pottery from the Nagsabaran site in northern [[Luzon|Luzon]]. Lapita people intermarried with Papuan populations and are the direct ancestors of the Austronesian peoples of [[Polynesia|Polynesia]]. The name comes from the type site in [[New Caledonia|New Caledonia]], excavated in 1952. More than 200 Lapita sites have been uncovered, ranging more than 4,000 km from Melanesia to Fiji and Tonga, with the most eastern limit in Samoa.

Differential operator defined as the divergence of the gradient of a scalar function. It is written ∇² or Δ and, in Cartesian coordinates, equals the sum of the second partial derivatives. The Laplacian of a function at a point measures how far its value there differs from its average over small surrounding spheres. Named after [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Pierre-Simon Laplace]], who applied it to celestial mechanics, it appears in the [[Heat equation|heat equation]], the [[Wave equation|wave equation]] and the [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger equation]] of quantum mechanics.

Second-order partial differential equation, named after [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Pierre-Simon Laplace]], who first studied its properties. Written ∇²f = 0 or Δf = 0, it states that the [[Laplace operator|Laplace operator]] of a function is zero. Its twice continuously differentiable solutions, called harmonic functions, are important in electrostatics, gravitation and [[Fluid dynamics|fluid dynamics]]. If the right-hand side is a given function, the equation becomes Poisson's equation, which generalizes it. Laplace's equation describes equilibrium, or situations that do not depend on time, and it is the steady-state [[Heat equation|heat equation]]. Its general theory is known as potential theory. The Dirichlet problem fixes boundary values, while the Neumann problem prescribes normal derivatives on the boundary.

Integral transform that converts a function of time into a function of a complex variable s. For suitable functions f it is defined by the integral ℒ{f}(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^(−st) dt. The transform turns differentiation and integration into multiplication and division, and [[Convolution|convolution]] into multiplication, so [[Differential equation|linear differential equations]] become algebraic equations that can be solved and then transformed back. For example, the equation of a simple harmonic oscillator becomes algebraic with its initial conditions included. It is closely related to the [[Fourier transform|Fourier transform]]. Its name honors [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Pierre-Simon Laplace]], who used a similar transform in his work on probability theory.

Semi-solid white fat rendered from the fatty tissue of a pig. It is distinguished from tallow, which comes from cattle or sheep. Lard can be rendered by steaming, boiling or dry heat, and if properly rendered it is nearly odorless and tasteless. It has a high saturated fat content but no trans fat. Leaf lard, from the fat around the kidneys and inside the loin, is the highest grade and is valued for flaky pie crusts. Lard was widely used in place of [[Butter|butter]] in North America and Europe, and as a butter substitute during [[World War II|World War II]]. From the early 1900s, vegetable shortenings and oils largely replaced it, though many cooks still favor it for [[Pastry|pastry]] and [[Sausage|sausages]]. Production is led by [[China|China]], followed by [[Germany|Germany]], [[Brazil|Brazil]], the United States and [[Russia|Russia]].

World's largest and highest-energy [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerator]], built by [[CERN|CERN]] near [[Geneva|Geneva]]. Built between 1998 and 2008 with more than 10,000 scientists, it lies in a tunnel 27 km (17 mi) in circumference beneath the France–Switzerland border. It primarily collides proton beams, though it also accelerates heavy ions such as lead. The [[Higgs boson|Higgs boson]] was announced in 2012, and its detection completed the [[Standard Model|Standard Model]] of particle physics. Other experiments test predictions of [[Supersymmetry|supersymmetry]] and search for [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and extra dimensions. First collisions took place in 2010 at 3.5 tera-electronvolts (TeV) per beam, and after upgrades the beams reached 6.5 TeV.

[[Dwarf galaxy|Dwarf galaxy]] and satellite of the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]], about 163,000 light-years away. It is the second- or third-closest galaxy to the Milky Way and the fourth-largest in the [[Local Group|Local Group]], with roughly one-hundredth the mass of the Milky Way. It is about 32,200 light-years across. Its off-center stellar bar suggests it was once a barred spiral, disrupted by tidal interactions with the [[Small Magellanic Cloud|Small Magellanic Cloud]] and the Milky Way. It is predicted to merge with the Milky Way in about 2.4 billion years. Visible as a faint cloud from the Southern Hemisphere, it straddles the constellations Dorado and Mensa. In 2025 the Center for Astrophysics reported strong evidence for a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] within it.

Last part of the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]] and digestive system in [[Tetrapod|tetrapods]], also called the large bowel. Water and salts are absorbed here, and remaining waste is stored in the rectum as feces before [[Defecation|defecation]]. Although shorter than the [[Small intestine|small intestine]], it is wider, and in humans it is about 1.5 m (5 ft) long. Its sections are the cecum, colon, rectum and anal canal, and the colon is divided into ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid parts. The [[Appendix (anatomy)|appendix]] develops from the cecum and contains lymphoid tissue. Gut bacteria ferment undigested material in the colon, producing some [[Vitamin|vitamins]]. About 1.5 liters of water reach the colon each day.

Type of [[Machine learning|machine learning]] model, typically a neural network, trained on vast amounts of text. LLMs can generate, summarize, translate and analyze text, and they underlie many modern [[Chatbot|chatbots]], such as [[ChatGPT|ChatGPT]]. Most are based on the transformer architecture, introduced by Google researchers in 2017. Generative pre-trained transformers are pretrained to predict the next word and are then fine-tuned to follow instructions. Biased or inaccurate training data makes output less reliable. A software harness can give a model memory and access to tools such as web search, which reduce but do not eliminate factual errors. Benchmark evaluations attempt to measure reasoning, factual accuracy, alignment and safety.

Soviet former artistic gymnast, born in Kherson. Between 1956 and 1964 she won 14 individual Olympic medals and four team medals for the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]]. Her nine Olympic gold medals are the record for a female gymnast, and her total of 18 Olympic medals was a record for 48 years. She debuted at the 1956 [[Olympic Games|Olympic Games]] in Melbourne, winning the all-around title, and in 1960 she led the Soviet team to victory in Rome. She also won the all-around title at the 1962 World Championships. Her father was killed at the [[Battle of Stalingrad|Battle of Stalingrad]], and she trained in [[Kyiv|Kyiv]].

[[Passerine|Passerine]] bird of the family Alaudidae. Larks are small to medium-sized, from 12 to 24 cm long, and most species have streaked brown plumage that provides [[Camouflage|camouflage]] on the ground, along with long hind claws. The family has a cosmopolitan distribution, with the largest number of species in Africa; only the horned lark occurs in North America. Many species live in drier regions. Adults of most species eat seeds, but all feed their young [[Insect|insects]] for at least the first week after hatching. The family contains 98 living species in 24 [[Genus|genera]]. When the word lark is used without qualification, it often refers to the Eurasian skylark.

American basketball player, coach and executive in the [[National Basketball Association|National Basketball Association]]. Bird played his entire 13-season playing career for the [[Boston Celtics|Boston Celtics]], winning three NBA championships and three consecutive Most Valuable Player awards from 1984 to 1986. He was a 12-time All-Star and a member of the 1992 U.S. Olympic team known as the Dream Team. He later coached the Indiana Pacers from 1997 to 2000 and served as their president of basketball operations, and he was named Executive of the Year for the 2012 season.

American comedian, writer, actor and television producer. With [[Jerry Seinfeld|Jerry Seinfeld]], he created the NBC sitcom *Seinfeld*. He later created, wrote and starred in the [[HBO|HBO]] series *Curb Your Enthusiasm*, which ran from 2000 to 2024. Known for his dry wit and portrayals of awkward social situations, he wrote briefly for [[Saturday Night Live|Saturday Night Live]] and since 2015 has appeared on it impersonating [[Bernie Sanders|Bernie Sanders]]. He has acted in three films directed by [[Woody Allen|Woody Allen]].
